threads.thread_goal: Align on target segments and top cross-sell opportunities for Q3.

messages.text: Kicking off segmentation for the Q3 cross-sell playbook for project_pack_ref: Launch of Cross-Sell Sales Playbook for Q3. For T1 and T4 we need to lock the list of target customer segments and the top 3 cross-sell opportunities per segment so we can populate A1. My initial proposal: 1) Mid-market existing customers with at least one core product; 2) Enterprise accounts with renewals in the next 6 months; 3) SMB customers on single-product contracts. For each, we would define 3 priority cross-sell pairings based on current attach rates and margin. Can you react to this proposal and suggest adjustments before we formalize D1 and D2

Thanks for framing this. From what we see in the field, I agree with the three segments, but I would refine the second one to enterprise accounts with renewals in the next 9 months so we have enough pipeline to impact Q3. For cross-sell pairings, my quick view: Mid-market: add analytics, premium support, and training packages to core subscriptions. Enterprise: add security add-ons, multi-region deployment, and consulting. SMB: bundle basic analytics, onboarding package, and small seat expansions. We should validate these against margin and discount rules later, but they are a good starting point for A1 under T4.

I like the structure. One concern: SMB single-product customers can be very price sensitive. For them, cross-sell works better when we position it as solving a concrete problem, not just an add-on. I would suggest we split SMB into: a) growing SMBs with usage trending up; b) stable or declining SMBs. For group a), cross-sell could be seat expansion plus onboarding support; for group b), maybe only low-friction add-ons like basic analytics. That might complicate A1 a bit, but it will make T1 more realistic.

Jumping in with a data angle. Before we finalize D1, I would like to check how these segments map to existing CRM fields so we do not create something we cannot filter. For example, do we already tag growing SMBs vs stable SMBs, or would we need to infer that from usage or revenue growth. For T1, I can pull a quick snapshot of current attach rates and deal sizes by the three proposed segments using what we already have, then we can see if the SMB split is feasible for A1.

Good point on CRM mapping. From previous projects, we usually had segment fields for SMB, mid-market, and enterprise, plus renewal date and product mix. We did not have a direct flag for growing vs stable SMBs, but we could approximate with revenue trend or seat count change. For the purpose of D1, maybe we keep SMB as one segment in the official list, and in A1 we note a sub-priority for growing SMBs where data is available. That way T1 stays aligned with current CRM structure.

Agree on not overcomplicating the official segmentation. How about this: D1 would list three main segments as proposed: SMB, mid-market, enterprise. Inside A1, for SMB we add a note that the primary focus is on accounts with positive usage or revenue trend, and we give guidance on how to identify them in CRM. That keeps T1 and T4 manageable and still reflects your field insight.

Works for me. For the top 3 cross-sell opportunities per segment for D2, I suggest we keep it simple and focused on what reps already know how to sell. For example: SMB: 1) seat expansion, 2) basic analytics, 3) onboarding package. Mid-market: 1) analytics, 2) premium support, 3) training. Enterprise: 1) security add-ons, 2) consulting, 3) multi-region deployment. We can refine wording later in the playbook, but this gives T4 a clear direction.

I ran a quick check on last quarter deals. The pairings you listed line up with where we already see traction, and they respect the constraint of no changes to the core pricing model. One nuance: for enterprise consulting, we should probably frame it as packaged advisory tied to cross-sell, not open-ended projects, to avoid scope creep. I will note that in A1 under T4 so it is clear for later playbook drafting.

Sounds like we are converging. To close D1, can we confirm that the official target segments for the Q3 playbook are: 1) SMB existing customers on single-product contracts; 2) Mid-market existing customers with at least one core product; 3) Enterprise accounts with renewals in the next 9 months. Within SMB, A1 will highlight growing accounts as priority where data allows. If there are no objections by end of day, I will record this as D1 and move T1 to done.

No objections from my side. The three segments are clear and match how we usually slice the pipeline. The only suggestion is to make sure we document the assumptions in A1 for T1, especially the 9-month renewal window for enterprise, so finance and marketing can reuse the same definition later.

Confirmed from sales side as well. The three segments and the top 3 cross-sell pairings per segment work for us. Once A1 is updated under T4, we can use it as the base for messaging and qualification criteria in the playbook.

I will take the action to update A1 with the agreed segments and the three cross-sell pairings per segment, plus the notes on SMB growth focus and enterprise consulting scope. Once done, I will share a link here so everyone can double-check before we move on to drafting the playbook under T2.

threads.thread_goal: Review and finalize the first version of the cross-sell playbook.

messages.text: I have uploaded A2, the first draft of the cross-sell sales playbook, based on the segments and pairings we locked in A1 and T1/T4. The structure covers: 1) qualification checklist by segment, 2) discovery questions, 3) recommended offers, 4) CRM steps, and 5) follow-up and tracking aligned with A3 and T5. I need your feedback on two points: a) is the structure right for D3, and b) does the CRM section reflect the current workflow for D4, especially around opportunity stages and fields. Please add comments or reply here with any gaps.

Thanks for pulling A2 together. Overall the flow feels intuitive from a rep perspective. One thing I would adjust: in the qualification checklist, we might be asking for too many data points before a rep can move forward. For example, for SMB we probably do not need a full budget confirmation before suggesting a small analytics add-on. Could we simplify that section so we do not slow down deals, in line with the project constraint about not overcomplicating the process

I agree with the overall structure for D3. The discovery questions are strong, especially for mid-market and enterprise. For SMB, I would add one or two questions about growth plans and upcoming initiatives, since that is how we spot cross-sell potential. Also, in the recommended offers section, can we make it very clear which pairings are primary vs optional, matching the top 3 in A1, so reps do not get lost in too many options

On the CRM side for D4, I walked through the steps in A2 against our current workflow. The mapping to opportunity stages looks fine, but there are two fields you marked as mandatory that are currently optional in CRM: cross-sell type and attach product. If we want to make them mandatory, we will need approval from the CRM admin and probably a small change request. To stay within T3 and the project constraints, I suggest we keep them as recommended fields in the playbook and only flag them as mandatory once we have formal approval.

Good catch. We cannot unilaterally change mandatory fields. For D4, the requirement is that the playbook aligns with existing workflows, not the other way around. Let us adjust A2 so that cross-sell type and attach product are clearly recommended, and we add a note that making them mandatory is under review with the CRM admin as a separate track. That keeps T3 within scope.

On the qualification checklist, I can trim it down. For SMB, we can reduce it to three core checks: 1) product fit, 2) basic budget sense, and 3) timing. Detailed budget confirmation can move to later in the process. For mid-market and enterprise, we keep the fuller checklist but mark some items as nice-to-have. I will update A2 accordingly so we do not slow down cycles, and I will highlight the change in the next version.

Good point on primary vs optional offers. I will align the recommended offers section in A2 with the top 3 pairings per segment from A1 and T4, and visually separate primary offers from optional ones. That should help reps focus on the highest impact options first.

That adjustment on the checklist works. One more suggestion: in the follow-up and tracking section, can we reference the key KPIs from A3 and T5, so reps understand why we are asking them to log certain fields. For example, if we are tracking cross-sell conversion rate by segment, we should say that explicitly.

Agree. In A3 we already defined cross-sell pipeline volume, win rate, and average deal size by segment as core KPIs. If we reference those in A2, it will make the dashboard story more coherent. For T5, I can add a short explanation in A3 about which CRM fields feed each KPI, and we can mirror that language in the playbook.

Perfect. I will update the tracking section in A2 to reference the KPIs from A3 and clarify which fields are essential for those metrics. That should also help with adoption, since reps will see the link between their admin work and the dashboard.

To move towards D3, here is how I see the final structure of A2: 1) Segment overview and when to use the playbook; 2) Qualification checklist by segment; 3) Discovery questions; 4) Recommended offers with primary and optional pairings; 5) CRM steps aligned with current workflow; 6) Follow-up and KPI tracking linked to A3. If everyone is comfortable with this outline, we can lock D3 once the edits discussed above are in.

This structure works for me. It is close to how reps think through a conversation, and the CRM and KPI sections are not too heavy. Once the simplifications on the SMB checklist and the primary offers are in A2, I am fine considering D3 closed.
Same here. The outline is clear, and the adjustments we discussed address my concerns about complexity. From sales side, we can go ahead with D3 once the updated A2 is shared.

I will incorporate all feedback and publish A2 v1.1 by end of day, with the simplified SMB checklist, primary vs optional offers aligned to A1, and the CRM and KPI clarifications. Once that is out, we can formally treat D3 and D4 as closed for this iteration and move on to pilot planning under T6.

threads.thread_goal: Define pilot scope, participants, and success criteria.

messages.text: Time to define the pilot for the cross-sell playbook. For T6, my proposal is: scope: use A2 with one mid-market sales team and a small group of SMB reps; duration: 4 weeks starting two weeks before Q3; success metrics: cross-sell opportunities created, win rate, and average deal size uplift vs baseline, using the KPIs in A3. For feedback (T7 and A5), we would run a short survey plus two group interviews. We also need to confirm D5 (which team and duration) and D6 (success metrics and feedback approach). Thoughts

From sales side, I suggest we focus the pilot on one mid-market pod and a subset of SMB reps who are already comfortable with cross-sell. That will give us cleaner feedback on the playbook itself, not on basic selling skills. Four weeks sounds reasonable for D5, but we should make sure we are not overlapping with any major campaigns that could distort the numbers.

Agree on using one mid-market team and a few SMB reps. I can volunteer my mid-market pod for the pilot, as long as we keep the admin overhead light. For D6, I would add one more metric: percentage of pilot reps actively using the playbook, maybe measured by how many cross-sell opportunities have the recommended fields filled in. That will help us catch adoption issues early.

On the admin side, we can keep the survey in A5 very short, maybe 5 questions, and use a simple template for the group interviews. For T7, I can help structure the feedback form so we capture both usability of A2 and any CRM friction. That should keep the time commitment reasonable for your team.

From a tracking perspective, using the KPIs in A3 for D6 makes sense. We can set up a simple dashboard view just for the pilot group, showing cross-sell opportunities created, win rate, average deal size, and the adoption metric suggested by 468837. That will also make it easier to compile A5 later.

Great that your pod can join the pilot. For D5, let us define it as: one mid-market pod led by 468837 plus 5 SMB reps nominated by 231, for a duration of 4 weeks. Start date would be two weeks before Q3, so we have time to adjust A2 before full launch. If that works, I will document it in T6.

Works for me. I can nominate 5 SMB reps who are already doing some cross-sell and are usually responsive to feedback requests. I will confirm the names by tomorrow so you can include them in T6 and in the invites.

On success metrics for D6, should we set explicit targets or just look for uplift vs baseline. Given this is a short pilot, I would lean towards directional uplift, for example: at least 10 percent increase in cross-sell opportunities created and a small bump in average deal size, rather than hard targets that might be unrealistic.

I agree. For a 4-week pilot, it is safer to define success as uplift vs each team’s own baseline, using the last quarter as reference in A3. We can say that the pilot is successful if we see a clear positive trend in opportunities created and average deal size, plus at least 70 percent of pilot reps using the playbook regularly. I will reflect that in the draft of A5.

Those criteria sound fair. The 70 percent usage threshold is ambitious but doable if we keep the playbook practical. Just make sure the survey in A5 also asks what would make reps use it more often, so we get concrete ideas for improvement.

To summarize for D6: success metrics will be uplift in cross-sell opportunities created and average deal size vs baseline, plus at least 70 percent of pilot reps using the playbook, measured via CRM fields and survey responses. Feedback collection will be a short survey and two group interviews, documented in A5 under T7. If there are no objections, I will treat D6 as agreed.

threads.thread_goal: Lock training approach, rollout checklist, and launch communication.

messages.text: With the pilot scope defined, we need to lock the training and launch plan for full rollout. I have drafted A6 (training and rollout checklist) and A7 (launch communication pack) based on T8, T10, and T11. Proposal: training format: 60-minute virtual session per team, plus a short self-serve guide; timing: one week before Q3 start; content: overview of A2, key KPIs from A3, and discount and approval rules from A4. For D7 we need to agree on format and timeline, and for D8 we need to sign off on the communication content and owners. Please review and share any concerns.

From a sales manager perspective, 60 minutes per team is acceptable if we keep it focused. I would suggest we split the session into: 1) why this matters (5–10 minutes), 2) how to use A2 in real calls (30 minutes with examples), 3) CRM and KPIs (10–15 minutes), 4) Q and A. Also, we should be careful not to overload the week before Q3 with too many meetings, so we might need to stagger sessions across a few days.

Agree on the structure. For D7, I would also like a short follow-up touchpoint two weeks into Q3, maybe a 30-minute clinic per region to address questions that come up after reps try A2. That could be part of A6 as an optional step but will help with adoption.

On A7 and T11, the launch communication looks solid. I would just make sure we clearly state what is changing for reps and what is not. For example, core pricing and discount thresholds remain the same, but the way we identify and track cross-sell is more structured. Also, we should mention that A4 is the single source of truth for discount and approval rules, so people know where to look.

Good call. We need to be explicit that we are not changing the pricing model, only standardizing cross-sell behavior. For D8, I propose that 231 owns the main email to sales teams, I own the project overview section, and 173966 owns the part about A2 and A6. That division of ownership should be reflected in A7 and T11.

I can adjust A6 to reflect that breakdown of the 60-minute session and add the optional 30-minute clinic suggested by 468837. For scheduling, we can propose a standard slot per region and let local managers shift within a 3-day window if needed. That should keep the calendar manageable while still meeting the D7 timeline.

Happy to own the main email in A7. I will emphasize the benefits for reps: higher deal sizes, clearer guidance, and less back-and-forth on approvals thanks to A4. I will also include the training dates from A6 so people can block their calendars.

From the field, the key is to keep the training practical. In A6, can we explicitly include two or three real call scenarios per segment where we walk through how to use A2 live. That will make it easier for reps to connect the dots.

Yes, I will add a section in A6 for segment-specific scenarios and coordinate with you to pick examples from recent deals. That will also help us later when we prepare the post-launch report in A8, since we can reuse some of those stories.

On T10, I reviewed A4 and the way it is referenced in A2 and A7. The governance for discounts and approvals is consistent with current policy. We just need to make sure we do not restate the rules in too much detail in the email; instead, we should link to A4 and highlight only the key thresholds and the exceptions process.

To close D7, I propose we confirm: training format is a 60-minute virtual session per team with a clear agenda plus an optional 30-minute clinic two weeks into Q3; rollout timeline is the week before Q3 start, with flexibility of a 3-day window per region; content is focused on why, how to use A2, CRM and KPIs from A3, and key rules from A4. If everyone agrees, we can mark D7 as approved and finalize A6 under T8.

I am aligned with that plan. From sales side, the format and timing are workable, and the content focus is right. We can proceed with D7 and D8 as described, and I will start tailoring the email in A7 today.

threads.thread_goal: Review early Q3 results and agree on improvement actions.

messages.text: We now have the first 4 weeks of Q3 data and a draft of A8 for review, based on T12. Using the KPIs defined in A3, we see: cross-sell opportunities created up 18 percent in mid-market and 9 percent in SMB; average deal size up 7 percent in mid-market and flat in SMB; adoption of A2 at around 65 percent of active reps. We need to agree on which improvement actions to prioritize for D9. Initial ideas: 1) simplify SMB flows in A2; 2) add more examples for enterprise deals; 3) tighten the link between CRM fields and dashboard views. Please share your read of the data and any other suggestions.

From conversations with managers, the mid-market uplift matches what we are hearing: the playbook is helping structure cross-sell conversations. In SMB, reps say the flow is still a bit heavy for small deals, which might explain the flat deal size. I support prioritizing simplification of SMB steps in A2 and maybe adjusting the messaging to focus more on quick wins.

On adoption, 65 percent is not bad for a first month but below the 70 percent we aimed for in D6. Feedback from my team is that they like A2 but sometimes forget to open it during calls. A quick improvement could be to add a short cheat sheet or one-pager per segment that they can keep open in parallel, and maybe a reminder in CRM when they create a cross-sell opportunity.

Looking at A3 and A8, one issue is that some dashboard views are not very intuitive for frontline reps. They see the numbers but are not sure what to do differently. I would prioritize tightening the link between CRM fields and dashboard views, and adding a short interpretation guide in A8 or as an appendix to A2, so managers can coach based on the data.

On the cheat sheet idea, we can create a condensed version of A2 per segment and attach it to A6 as an optional resource. That should help with in-call usage without changing the core playbook. For the CRM reminder, we would need to check with the CRM admin, but we can at least add a simple checklist in A6 for managers to reinforce during team meetings.

I like the idea of an interpretation guide. Managers have been asking how to translate the dashboard in A3 into coaching actions. If we add a simple section in A8 with examples like: if cross-sell opportunities are high but win rate is low, focus on qualification; if volume is low, focus on pipeline generation, that would be very helpful.

For SMB simplification, I would remove one or two steps that are more suited to larger deals, like detailed ROI calculations, and instead give reps a couple of quick value statements they can use. That should make it easier to upsell small analytics or onboarding packages without slowing them down.

Agreed. I can propose a lighter SMB path in A2 that removes the heavier steps and adds a few concise value statements, then we can test it with a small group before rolling it out broadly. I will also flag in A8 that this is a key improvement action so leadership understands the rationale.

I can take the lead on drafting that interpretation guide section in A8, using the KPIs from A3 as the backbone. We will keep it to one page with a few if-then examples so it is easy to use in team meetings.

Based on the discussion, I suggest we prioritize three improvement actions for D9: 1) simplify the SMB flow in A2 and add quick value statements; 2) create segment cheat sheets and add them to A6 to boost adoption; 3) add a dashboard interpretation guide in A8 linked to A3. Other ideas, like CRM reminders, we can park until we have capacity and admin approval.
I am aligned with those three priorities. They address the main pain points we are hearing from the field and should help move SMB results and adoption closer to where we want them.
Same here. If we can get the simplified SMB path and cheat sheets out quickly, I can pilot them with my team and share feedback for the next update of A2 and A8.
